content: When the sprue former slightly protrudes from the investment material, it creates a channel that connects the external environment to the investment pattern. This investment pattern is then placed in a simple centrifuge, where small amounts of gold are melted and rapidly forced through the channel in the investment pattern, passing through the sprue formed by the sprue former, and into the hollow space previously occupied by the wax pattern of the crown. This process is known as the lost-wax technique. Once the gold has cooled properly, the single-piece crown and sprue are separated, and the sprue can be recycled for use in another casting. The crown is then refined at the site of the sprue attachment, finished, polished to a high shine, and delivered to the dentist. The dentist tries the crown in the patient’s mouth, ensuring it has proper contact with adjacent and opposing teeth, and cements it onto the prepared tooth. Porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crowns consist of a metal coping created using the same lost-wax technique as full gold crowns. This coping is then prepared for the application of feldspathic porcelain. The coping may be designed to fit the dimensions of the restored tooth except for the facial surface, or it may be a thin shell intended to be fully covered with porcelain. Alternatively, it may be partially cut back to allow porcelain coverage only on the facial and occlusal surfaces. The alloy used for PFMs differs from that used for full gold crowns because it must withstand the high temperatures of the ceramic furnace without deforming or compromising the structural integrity of the metal coping. In some cases, the dentist may check the fit of the coping on the tooth before the porcelain is applied, while in other cases, the laboratory completes the PFM and returns it to the dentist after the porcelain application. A coping try-in is more common in cases involving multiple attached units or long-span bridges, where adjustments may be needed to ensure proper fit. The strength provided by cast metal restorations is a significant advantage, as it allows for conservation of tooth structure. When porcelain is added to occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth or proximal surfaces of anterior teeth, at least 1 mm of space must be reserved for the porcelain, in addition to the 0.5 mm required for the coping thickness. Porcelain is incorporated into restorations solely for aesthetic purposes, as its inclusion can compromise the strength and durability of the crown. The In-Ceram system, introduced in 1989 by Vita, enhanced the fragile all-ceramic crown by infusing it with glass, creating what was considered a superior product at the time. The Procera AllCeram system, owned by Nobel Biocare, is a CAD/CAM-based method that produces crowns by overlaying a durable ceramic coping, made of alumina or zirconia (referred to as the core), with Vitadur Alpha porcelain. Introduced in 1991, Procera can now be used to fabricate crowns, bridges, and veneers. The Empress system resembles the lost-wax technique in that it involves creating a hollow investment pattern. However, instead of casting metal, a specially designed pressure-injected leucite-reinforced ceramic is pressed into the mold, effectively casting the final all-ceramic restoration. The Empress system can be used for any application suitable for the lost-wax technique, as well as for veneers, which are not typically made of cast metal. The CEREC system, developed by Sirona Dental, is a method for fabricating all-ceramic restorations using digital technology. It captures a photographic image of the prepared tooth and uses computer software to design a 3D restoration that meets the specifications for an inlay, onlay, or single-unit crown, eliminating the need for traditional impressions. After finalizing the design, the dentist sends the data to a local milling machine, which uses diamond burs to mill the restoration from a solid ceramic ingot of a pre-selected shade. The process takes approximately 20 minutes, after which the dentist separates the restoration from the remaining ingot and tries it in the patient’s mouth. If the fit is satisfactory, the restoration can be cemented immediately. A CEREC machine costs approximately $100,000, with ongoing expenses for ceramic ingots and milling burs. Over 95% of restorations made using CEREC and Vita Mark I and Mark II blocks remain clinically successful after five years, and at least 90% are still functional after ten years. Advantages of Mark II blocks include wear rates similar to natural teeth, failure loads comparable to natural teeth, and wear patterns against enamel that mimic enamel-on-enamel interactions.
